addStarSystem.heading: The Star
addStarSystem.text: The Star The first thing we need to do is add the star itself. The star is the main focus of the star system and where all other points of interest are in orbit. Draw a circle in the middle of the hex and draw a line through its middle for its equator (see example right). It can be any size, but leave plenty of room around the edges for points of interest and potential jump lanes. You will also need to make it big enough to add the star system's threat level above its equator and a letter and reward adjustment below.

addStarSystem.heading: Name and Plane
addStarSystem.text: Name and Plane Next, we must name our star system. For convenience each star system's name in each sector (hex sheet) begins with a different letter of the alphabet (ranging from A-X). Using the sector's Star Systems & Zones sheet you are free to pick any letter that has not yet been taken and then roll on table (GB) N - Names using the "Star System" column; first roll using the "Prefix Column" and then the "Suffix Column". You then add the first letter you chose for the star system to the Prefix result and then add the Suffix result to complete the star system's name. Example: Jacob is naming a new star system. He looks on the sector's Star Systems & Zones sheet and sees "Q" is free, so decides the new star system's name will begin with the letter "Q". He next rolls twice on table (GB) N - Names. His first roll is 96 and he looks up the result using the Star System prefix column, it shows "ine". Next he rolls a 45 and on the Star System suffix column shows a result of "ust". He puts it all together for a final name of Qineust (Q + ine + ust). Once a name has been generated add it to the Star Systems & Zones sheet. Next, before we add the star system's name to the hex sheet we must determine the height at which the star system is located, in relation to the hex sheet. The hex sheet is flat and represents a zero height plane (a flat area of space); however, star systems are not always located on the same plane. The 3D drawing (below) of a hex sheet helps explain this by showing various star systems above and below the zero height plane (i.e. the hex sheet). It also shows one located on the zero height plane (the blue star system with the -20 threat level). To further explain take a look at the diagram below, it shows how the hex sheet will look on edge. The horizontal black line shows the edge of the hex sheet and now we can clearly see those star systems that are above, below, and at zero height plane. However, because we are mapping our sector in two dimension (to a flat hex sheet), we need a way to record which star systems are above the zero height plane, which star systems are below the zero height plane, and which star systems are on the zero height plane; and we also need to know by how much. We can do this by giving each star system a "Distance Marker". A star system with a positive distance marker is above the zero height plane, a star system with a negative value is below the zero height plane, and a star system with a zero value is actually on the zero height plane. To find out the star system's distance marker, it's simply a case of rolling 1d100 and 1d6 on table (GB) DM - Distance Marker and cross referencing the results. The number you generate will be a value between -299 and +299. The value is the number of light years the star system is from the zero height plane. When you have generated the distance marker you can go ahead and add the star system's name, along with its distance marker, to the hex sheet. To make a visual difference between plane positions, you can if you like write them in green for star systems above the zero height plane, in red for star systems below the zero height plane, and in black for star systems that are at a zero height plane. Note: If you are using the "Alternative Light Years" rules on page 11, you do not need to use distance markers at all and can simply add the star system's name to the hex sheet in black (or any colour you like). Example: Jacob is determining the distance marker for the star system Qineust. He rolls 1d100 and 1d6 on table (GB) DM - Distance Marker. He rolls a 32 on the d100 and a 1 on the d6. He cross references the two results on the table and find the star system is -113 light years from the zero plane. He adds the distance marker to the end of the star system's name and it now reads "Qineust -113". He adds the name to the hex sheet in red as it is below the zero height plane. 10

addStarSystem.heading: Threat Level
addStarSystem.text: Threat Level Next we must determine the star system's threat level. Roll 1d100 on table (GB) S - Star Systems and cross reference the result with the column named "Threat Level". Then shade in the star you drew in step 1 using the colour of the threat you rolled. Lastly add the star system's threat level above the equator line. In the diagram above the player generated a Terrifying Threat Level and has added the star system's threat level. If you don't want to use colour you can just add the star system's threat level above the equator line and leave the shading. Also, add the star system's threat level to the Star Systems & Zones sheet.

addStarSystem.heading: Reward Adjust
addStarSystem.text: Reward Adjust Some star systems are particularly wealthy and monetary value is excessively high, whilst other star systems are relatively poor with a struggling economy. This is going to be reflected when you interact with a star system. To determine a star system's reward adjustment, roll 1d100 and look up the result on table (GB) S - Star Systems using the "Reward Adjust $" column; this is the star system's reward adjustment. Add the first letter of the star system and its reward adjustment to the star, below its equator. On the diagram above, captain Jacob rolled a 91. Using the "Reward Adjust $" column on table (GB) S - Star Systems, he looked up the result of 91, which showed a "Corporate +3 $" reward adjustment. Jacob added the first letter of the star system's name and the Reward Adjustment below the equator on the star on the hex sheet.

addStarSystem.heading: Jump Lanes
addStarSystem.text: Jump Lanes Star systems are linked via hyper jump lanes. Look over the hex sheet for other star systems that have an incomplete hyper jump lane that could be connected to the star system you're creating. If there is one or more, connect them to the new star system. On the diagram above right Jacob has added the green star system with the -10 modifier and can see the purple star system with the -40 modifier and the blue star system with the -30 modifier have incomplete hyper jump lanes that can connect to the star system he is creating. He completes the hyper jump lanes and connects the star systems together. If you are adding a star system, but there aren't any incomplete hyper jump lanes available to connect to the new star system; roll 1d6 and use the direction hex to determine an edge a hyper jump lane will begin from. Next, draw a line from the centre of the star to the edge of the hex. On the diagram to the right, Jacob has rolled a 2 and determined the direction of the lane using the direction hex. He then added a hyper jump lane from the centre of the new star system to the edge of the designated hex. After adding an incomplete hyper jump lane follow its path, if another star system is in its direction you connect the lane to the star system. On the diagram above, the yellow star system with the +5 threat level is in the path of the hyper jump lane and can connect. Jacob extends the hyper jump lane to the star system (shown on the diagram below). If the new star system's hyper jump lane doesn’t have a star system in its path, the hyper jump lane is left incomplete and you proceed to step 7. POIs.

addStarSystem.heading: Light Years
addStarSystem.text: Light Years If you have not added a completed hyper jump lane, you can skip this step and proceed to step 7. POIs. However, if you have added a completed hyper jump lane you will need to calculate the distance in light years between the connected star systems. Imagine two points in the air at different heights, we need to measure the distance between them. The diagram below shows the hex sheet in isometric with various hyper jump lanes added to connect the star systems. This demonstrates what we must achieve. 11 Begin by looking at the distance markers for the star systems you are connecting. We need to create a y value (the distance they are apart on a vertical plane). Use which of the follow options applies: If both star systems have a positive distance marker, or a negative distance marker, deduct the lower value from the higher value (ignoring + or -) for the y value. If one star system has a positive distance marker and the other a negative distance marker, add the two values together (ignoring + and -) for the y value. If one of the star systems is at zero height (i.e. it does not have a distance marker) and the other has a positive, or a negative distance marker then that distance marker is the y value. If both star systems are at a zero height plane (i.e. both have no distance marker) their y value is 0. Example: Jacob is connecting two star systems, one has a distance marker of +76 and the other has a distance marker of +98. Because they both have positive distance markers Jacob deducts 76 from 98 for a y value of 22 (98 - 76 = 22). Later Jacob is connecting two star systems with a -12 and a -45 distance marker. Because they both have negative distance markers Jacob deducts 12 from 45 for a y value of 23 (45 - 12 = 23). Later Jacob is connecting two star systems with a -67 and a +88 distance marker. Because one has a positive distance marker and the other has a negative distance marker Jacob adds the two distance markers together for a y value of a 155 (67 + 88 = 155). Later Jacob is connecting a star system with a distance marker of +48 to one that is on the zero height plane (i.e. it doesn’t have a distance marker), the y value is 48. Later Jacob is connecting two star systems that both have no distance markers (i.e. they both are on the zero height plane), the y value is 0. Next find the distance between the two star systems by counting hexes. The distance is measured in light years (see diagram). Each hex is the equivalent of 100 light years. This will provide you with a distance they are apart on a horizontal plane, we call this their x value. Next take the y value and the x value and cross reference them on table (GB) Hyper Jump Lane for the number of light years the jump lane is long, and add it to the hex sheet above or below the hyper jump lane on the hex sheet. Alternative Light Years If you prefer a simplified way of generating the distance of jump lanes, you can ignore the distance markers altogether and instead count up 100 light years for each hex between the star systems you're connecting. Then add to this 1d100 for each of those hexes. The result is the length of the jump lane in light years. Example: Jacob is connecting two star systems with a jump lane. As they are 4 hexes apart they are automatically 400 light years apart. Next he rolls 4d100 and adds them together (1d100 for each hex the two star systems are apart). He rolls 8, 20, 98, and 45 for a total of 171 (8+20+98+45=171). He adds the 171 to 400 for a final light year distance of 571 (171+400=571). Bisecting Jump Lanes Sometimes you will place a star system over the top of an existing jump lane. The lane is now linked to the new star system on both sides and the jump lane's distances must be recalculated. Example: Jacob is about to placed the -30 star system over a jump lane that is linking the -5 and -10 star systems together. When the -30 star system is placed it has bisected the jump lane and now all three star systems are linked. Jacob must recalculate the jump lanes A and B.

addStarSystem.heading: POIs
addStarSystem.text: POIs Next we must determine the number of points of interest within the star system, and their type. Roll on table (GB) S - Star Systems and cross reference the result with the column named "# POI"; the result is the number of points of interest within the star system. For each point of interest roll again on table (GB) S - Star Systems, but this time cross reference the result with the column named "Point of Interest". As you generate each point of interest add them to the hex around the star starting from the left to right and wrapping around the bottom (see the diagram above). Add them in strict order as they are generated. The following rules must be observed when generating POIs: If a result duplicates a point of interest that has already been added, ignore the result and roll again for another. Each star system may only have a military dock or a space station , never both. If you have already generated a military dock and then roll a space station (or vice versa) you must re-roll for another type of point of interest. If you have generated all of the points of interest and the star system does not have a military dock or a space station you must replace one of the points of interest (chosen at random) with either a military dock or a space station . Roll 1d6: on a result of 1-3 you replace a point of interest with a military dock ; on a result of 4-6 you replace a point of interest with a space station . If you generate a worm hole, you must determine where it will lead. This is done after step 9.Naming POIs, See Wormholes. If you wish to use colour you can shade the points of interest, otherwise make sure they are clearly marked with any lettering they require for identification (i.e. "M" for moons). Example: Jacob rolls for the number of POIs and scores 74. He cross references 74 with the "# POI" column and it shows there will be 4 POI. Next, he rolls for each using the "Point of Interest" column; he rolls a 14 for Gases, 85 for Moon, 42 for Agricultural World, and a 86 for another moon. As a Moon has already been generated, he must roll again and this time scores 65 for a Military Dock. He adds them in the order they were generated around the star, starting on the left (see diagram above). 12

addStarSystem.heading: Zones
addStarSystem.text: Zones Now we have our points of interest, we must add them to the Star Systems & Zones sheet. They are added to the zones in the order they have been added to the hex sheet around the star from left to right. First roll 1d100 on table (GB) S - Star systems and look up the result using the Z D100 column. Next look at the letters that follow and the columns of zones they appear in. These letters will indicate where the points of interest will be placed on the Star Systems & Zones sheet. However, if the star system has 5 or less points of interests, you will only use some of the letters to place the points of interest in and you roll on the table below to see which letters you will use. Then populate the zones on the Star Systems & Zones sheet. 1d100 1-16 17-33 34-50 51-66 67-83 84-100 3 POIs BCD DEF ADF ABF CDF BCE 4 POIs CDEF ADEF ABDE BCEF BCDF ABCE 5 POIs BCDEF ACDEF ABDEF ABCEF ABCDF ABCDE Example: Jacob rolls 1d100 and scores 49. He looks up the result on (GB) S - Star systems using the Z D100 column to find out which zones will be used for points of interest. As Jacob has 4 points of interest to place, he rolls 1d100 on the table above and scores 18. It shows he will use letters ADE and F. Letter B and C will not be used. Next he collates them to the zones on the Star Systems & Zones sheet using his result of 49 from table (GB) S - Star systems using the Z D100 column. He places Gases in zone 4 (using letter A), Moon in zone 8 (letter D), Agricultural World in zone 9 (letter E) and finally the military Dock in zone 10 (letter F). See the diagram at the bottom of this page.

addStarSystem.heading: Naming POIs
addStarSystem.text: Naming POIs Next, you must name the points of interest on the Star Systems & Zones sheet. For each one, roll twice on table (GB) N - Names using the "Points of interest" column; first roll using the "Prefix Column" and then the "Suffix Column". When you have the two results add the suffix to the prefix for its name. If you like, you can further detail the point of interest's name. This is especially helpful if you have already generated a similar name or the exact name somewhere else in the sector. The choices can be as simple as adding its zone reference (i.e. Modep IV or Modep 4, if it is located in zone 4), or you could add the position it is located within the points of interest on the hex sheet (i.e. Modep I or Modep 1, if it is the first point of interest in the line). You could also decide to give the point of interest a second name. This would simply require rolling and generated a second name using the same procedure as before; then you could add the new name before or after the first one you generated. Lastly, if the point of interest is a Space Station or a Military Dock, you could add "Station", "Colony", "Terminal", "Division", or "Base" after its name. The name of a point of interest does not have an impact on the mechanics of the game, so you're free to go wild and name them however you like. The most important part of the naming process is not to repeat the same name in the same sector of the galaxy. Example: Jacob has four points of interest he must name. Starting from left to right on the hex sheet, he rolls 1d100 twice for each and looks up the results using table (GB) N - Names. For the first point of interest in the line he scores 29 and 92. Looking them up using the "Points of Interest" column, he gets a result of "Mod" for the prefix column and "ep" for the suffix column. Adding them together he names the Gases point of interest "Modep". He continues rolling on the table and gets 79 and 27 for the Moon and names it "Copva", 53 and 62 for the Agricultural World and names it "Juddite". When he rolls for the Military Dock, he scores 53 and 94 giving it the name "Juddar". Deciding it is too similar to the Agricultural World's name, he adds "Base" after the name, and it becomes "Juddar Base". See the diagram at the bottom of this page.

addStarSystem.heading: The Economy
addStarSystem.text: The Economy Each star system has a pricing structure reflected by its reward adjustment. The last step to creating your star system is to add its buy and sell prices for cargo and its ship and modification modifier to the sector's economy sheet. You can do this by simply finding the star system's reward adjustment on table (GB) C - Cargo Prices and copying the buy and sell prices to the sector's economy sheet. The star systems are listed alphabetically on the star sheet. Write the star system's name in the correct slot on the sheet and fill in its prices. It is highly recommended you play the Galaxy Builder with the Changing Economy rules (see Changing Economy). If you decide to use the Changing Economy rules you can leave these prices blank on the economy sheet and only begin filling them in when you wish to check their prices during a port phase. However, still add the star system's name and its port to the economy sheet. 13

newGalaxy.heading: 1Take a blank hex sheet and write "001:" in the name box,
newGalaxy.text: Take a blank hex sheet and write "001:" in the name box, keep it towards the left of the box. Next roll 1d100 twice on table (GB) N - Names. Use the "Sector Prefix" column for the first roll, and the "Sector Suffix" Column for the second roll. The first result is going to be the start of the name, and the second is going to be the end of the name. Put the two names together to create the name of the sector and write it after the number in the name box. Alternatively to rolling, you're free to name the sector anything you like; names of sectors have no bearing on the game mechanics and are used purely for reference. Example: Jacob rolls 1d100 and scores 61. He looks up the result on table (GB) N - Names using the Sector Prefix column. The result show "Gav". He rolls again and scores 71, this time he looks up the result using the Sector Suffix column. The result reads "bark" he adds them together for a Sector name of "Gavbark". He adds "Gavbark" to the name box on the hex sheet.
With a new sector you must have somewhere to store its economy. Take a blank economy sheet and add the Sector's name and number to the "Sector Name" box on the sheet.

You must now create your home star system in one of the 3 central hex spaces on the hex sheet (see the diagram on the right). If you can't decide, roll 1d3 to choose randomly. When you have chosen the home hex, create the star system using the "Adding Star Systems" rules on page 9. When you have completed the home star system come back here and continue with step 4. Example: Jacob cannot decide which will be his home hex. He rolls 1d3 and scores 2. His home star system will be in hex two. Next, he follows the rules "Adding Star Systems" on page 9 and adds the Andere system.

We need to populate the sector with some other star systems. First follow the path of the incomplete hyper jump lane you added when creating your home star system and generate another star system in the hex adjacent (they are connected via the hyper jump lanes during the process). Next, roll 1d6 and using the direction hex generate another star system two hexes away from your home star system; this star system must be in a different direction to the last one you added, if it isn't you must roll for another direction. Whilst adding the star system, this time do not roll for a direction for the hyper jump lane; instead, connect it to your home star system and then work out the light year distance in the usual way following the instructions in step 6 of the rules "Adding Star Systems" on page 9. You will end up with three star systems in your sector: Your home star system and two others connected via hyper jump lanes. Example: Jacob follows the path of the incomplete hyper jump lane and creates another star system in the hex to the northeast (direction 1 on the direction hex). He extends the incomplete hyper jump lane from his home star system to the new star system. Next, he rolls 1d6 and scores a 2. The next star system will be due east and two hex spaces away. Jacob generates the new star system and connects it with a hyper jump lane to his home star system.

The sector is now starting to fill out a little. Next, in each of the star systems you've added so far there will be an operation. Operations are added to hex spaces using an operation code. The operation code allows us to can keep track of where they are in the sector. Each operation code begins with the letter “O” and is followed by a number ranging from 1-24. Their details are recorded on an "Operation Sheet". Because each hex sheet has a set of operations unique to its sector, it is very important to keep them together at all times. Therefore, it's recommended that the operation sheet is printed to the back of the hex sheet, so they cannot be separated from one another. You can go ahead and add "O1" to your home star system hex, then "O2" to the star system in the adjacent hex, and lastly "O3" to the star system 2 hex spaces away. You can add them anywhere in the hex space. With their location marked on the hex sheet, we must generate the operation's details; but first you'll need a time sheet to make note of the operation's expiry dates. The time sheet can be found at the back of this book and is available to download from www.mk-games.co.uk to print out; permission is also given for you to make copies from this book for your own personal use. When you have the time sheet, add "3000" to the star year box and place a cross (⊠) through the first day on the Star Date Chart. The starting date is 01.01.3000 (ignore the strigger day). With the time sheet prepared you can generate the operations; see Generating Operations on page 20 and follow the instructions for all three operations. For an easier start in the new galaxy, you can roll 1d10 (instead of a d100) when rolling of table (GB) O - Operations. When all three operations have been fully generated return here and perform step 5.
On page 121 you will find a new log sheet called “(GB) Log Sheet”; it includes some extra details unique to the Galaxy

generatingOperations.heading: 1Selecting A Star System: If you already know the star system
generatingOperations.text: Selecting A Star System: If you already know the star system where the operation is located you can skip this step and proceed to step 2; otherwise, please read on. Operations are always found within a star system. Using the star system and zone sheet roll the d100 for a random star system. The result will be the location of the operation. However, each star system may only contain one operation. Therefore, if the star system you have rolled, already has an operation (whether it be completed, incomplete, or not yet attempted) you must generate another star system for the operation's location. This can either be by making another roll, or using another random method of your own devising. Once a star system has been selected for the operation's location, check to see if it the system has been generated; if it has, you add its operation code to its hex on the hex sheet and then continue to step 2. If it has not, you must perform steps A-D below to locate the operation and its star system. Note: Operation codes are generated in order from 1-24. You can find the next available operation code by finding the next empty slot on the operation sheet. A.	 First we need to select the hex where the operation's star system is located. Roll 1d6, and uses the direction hex to determine its direction from the captain's current hex. B.	 Next, we need to know how far away the operation's star system is from the captain's current position. Roll 1d3, the result is the number of hex spaces you count in the direction you determined in step A. However, any star 21 systems that are in the direction are skipped and you do not count them. In addition, if the count would take the operation's star system off the hex sheet entirely, it is instead placed in the last available hex space (on the sheet). However, if this is not possible, because all hex spaces already have star systems, you must roll again for a new direction by repeating step A. On very rare occasions when all directions leading away from the captain's current hex space all contain a star system, and there are no empty hex spaces available, the captain does not get to add the operation and the generation process comes to an end. C.	 Once the hex for the operation's star system has been determined, you add its operation code to the hex space. You can find the next available operation code by finding the next empty slot on the operation sheet. Example: Jacob is in the Andere system and has just discovered the whereabouts of an operation. He rolls 1d6 and scores 2, the operation is somewhere to the east. Next he rolls 1d3 to determine how far away it is from his current location, he rolls a 3. He counts the hex spaces; however, because the Eloxdoo system already has an operation, its hex space is skipped, see below. Jacob adds the next available operation code from the operation sheet (which is O4) to the hex space. D.	 Lastly, we need to mark the position of the star system on the hex sheet. You do this by adding a blank star system along with the first letter of the star system's name. At this stage you do not generate the rest of the star system. Later in the game when you're able to perform the "Adding Star System" rules, you may choose the incomplete star system. Note: until the star system has been generated the operation is not reachable by the captain. Now go to step 2.

The Operation Number: Next roll on table (GB) O – Operations, and record the number you rolled in the “#” box on the operation sheet. This number is used as a reference to the operation and could be needed when performing the mission.

The Operation's Details: Read through the operation’s details, and record the bold information to the “Details” box (you will in most cases need to write two lines of details in the box). This is optional, but if you decide not to add the details, you'll find yourself needing to look over them on table O before making a selection of your next mission. (Hand In): Some operations show "(Hand In)", for these operations any items that are collected, or looted to complete the mission are not kept when the mission is completed successfully and must be removed from the log sheet (see Operations). [KEYWORD]: Keywords are shown within squared brackets, such as: [PORT], [ZONE #], and [SYSTEM]; and require you to replace them with the name of the point of interest, the zone number, or the star system's name when you're taking down the details or reading the operation's story text (shown in italics). Note: If a specific zone is not targeted by a mission with the [ZONE #] keyword you will need to generate a zone randomly, see Random Star Systems and Zones on page 14. [NPC]: If the operation has the keyword [NPC], you'll need to roll three times on table (GB) N – Names using the “NPC (Name, Surname, and Occupation)” columns to generate a non-player character (NPC). First use the "Name" column, then the "Surname" column, and lastly the "Occupation" column. You then replace the [NPC] keyword with the NPC's full name and occupation wherever it is shown in the details. In addition, if the NPC has a NPC$ adjustment, you add it to the NPC$ box on the operation sheet. Random Values: If the operation's details asks for a roll to determine a specific number of things in order to complete the operation, they are rolled as the details are being recorded, and not at the start of each operation attempt. Expire Date: Most operations have an expiry date shown with the [DATE] keyword. You generate a date in the future using the instructions provided and replace the [DATE] keyword with the generated date (i.e. 0.4.3000). Some operations never expire and have an expiry date of "N/A"; these missions remain available until completed. If the captain doesn’t complete the mission in time it's removed from the hex sheet, the operation sheet, and the star systems & zone sheet; then, the operation's slot (on the operation sheet), and its operation's number is once again available and can be used for the future missions.

Location: Add the first letter of the star system and its zone number where the operation is located in the "LOC" box. This is a handy reference to where to find an operation. Also add it to the Star Systems & Zone sheet.
Mission Bonus: Each mission has a Mission Bonus (M$). You add this to the “M$” box on the operation sheet.
Star System Bonus: Each mission has a Star System Bonus, this is in fact the star system's reward adjustment where the operation is located. Add this to the "S$” Box on the operation sheet.

The Reward Value: The reward value is a calculation of values recorded in the NPC$, M$, and S$ boxes. They are added or subtracted (where applicable) to establish a total. Go ahead and make the calculation and add the total to the “RV” box on the operation sheet.

Success and Failure: Lastly, roll 1d6 and look up the result on table (GB) OR - Operation Reward. You cross reference the result with the RV value you just recorded in step 7. You then fill in the missions “[S]”, and “[F]” details for the operation. Note: Space missions do not have a [F] penalty, so do not include them when generating a space mission. Example: Jacob's operation has an RV of 7. He rolls 1d6 and scores a 5. He cross references 5 with RV 7 on the (GB) OR - Operation Reward table to find the operation's success and failure details as: [S]+8000c [F] B-25. He adds the details to the [S] and [F] boxes on the operation sheet. 22 Performing Operations In the Galaxy Builder game you add operations to the hex sheet and to a specific zone within a star system. When the captain's starship is at a location (in the star system's zone) where an operation has been added they may attempt the mission. The mission is then played in the traditional way, as explained in the D100 Space rulebook, except if the operation is successful it is marked with a  on the hex sheet and ticked  in the check box on the operation sheet; the mission is then completed and may
